claims.text: Substituting approximately 5–6 mol% Hf for Zr in ZrB2 enhances densification during reactive spark plasma sintering at approximately 1650 °C.
The Hf-modified material can achieve nearly full densification at approximately 1650 °C.
Hf substitution enhances defect mobility during reactive spark plasma sintering.
Enhanced defect mobility enables full densification at a lower sintering temperature.
Reactive spark plasma sintering of the Hf-modified material produces a fine Hf-enriched grain-boundary network.
High-temperature exposure converts or develops the Hf-enriched grain-boundary network into a coherent mixed oxide scale composed primarily of HfO2 and ZrO2.
Hf segregation promotes nucleation of a continuous refractory Hf-rich oxide layer at grain boundaries.
The Hf-rich mixed oxide scale inhibits oxygen ingress.
The Hf-rich mixed oxide scale inhibits molten-metal ingress.
The proposed mixed oxide scale is more resistant to oxidation and corrosion than scales formed on undoped ZrB2 or earlier lower-temperature materials.
The Hf-modified ZrB2 will retain mechanical strength and structural integrity comparable to pure ZrB2 fabricated at high temperature.
After 10 hours in air at 1400 °C, the Hf-modified ZrB2 will exhibit slower oxidation weight gain and a stable protective scale.
The Hf-modified ZrB2 will show minimal interfacial degradation during exposure to molten tin.
Pure ZrB2 fabricated above 2300 °C has poorer high-temperature oxidation resistance than the proposed Hf-modified material.
Pure ZrB2 fabricated above 2300 °C has poorer liquid-metal corrosion performance than the proposed Hf-modified material.
Previously reported lower-temperature specimens did not form robust oxidation or liquid-metal corrosion barriers.
The proposed material is applicable in ambient oxidizing service up to 1400 °C.
The proposed material is applicable to molten tin or similar liquid plating-metal service.
A 5–6 mol% Hf substitution level can remain within the single-phase stability region of (Zr,Hf)B2.

contradictions.description: The pure-ZrB2 control is described as being processed under standard high-temperature conditions, but the design then says both groups receive identical RSPS conditions. This leaves it unclear whether the control is fabricated above 2300 °C or by the proposed approximately 1650 °C RSPS schedule.
The predicted outcome requires 'nearly full densification,' whereas the mechanism and falsification rule refer to 'full densification.' No numerical density criterion resolves this difference.
